key_insight: Finite-rate chemistry significantly changes hypersonic shock/turbulent boundary-layer interaction physics, while thermally vs. calorically perfect gas assumptions make only secondary differences.
engineering_relevance: For hypersonic vehicle design, using a frozen/chemically reacting model can materially affect predicted separation, wall heating, and shock structure, impacting thermal protection and load estimates.
method: 3 direct numerical simulations of an oblique shock impinging on a turbulent high-enthalpy boundary layer.
Compared finite-rate reactive chemistry against single-species thermally perfect and calorically perfect gas models.
Held geometry and freestream conditions fixed at Me = 6.4 and He = 16.9 MJ/kg to isolate thermochemical-model effects.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the reactive case yields a smaller separation bubble, lower post-interaction wall heat flux, lower mean/fluctuating temperatures, and a less inclined reflected shock than the simplified gas models.
watch_item: The conclusions are specific to this Mach/enthalpy regime and the chosen DNS setup, so extrapolation to other hypersonic conditions or wall/catalysis effects should be done cautiously.
paper_title: Effects of thermochemical modelling on a hypersonic shock-wave/turbulent boundary-layer interaction
